content:
Gambling is fun. Unless you lose. Unless-unless you were gambling with house money the whole time. In which case, who cares?

Hold that thought. Earlier this month, Monster Beverage Corporation (MBC) reported its earnings for the second quarter of 2026. They were pretty spectacular.

“Net sales, excluding the alcohol brand segment, increased 20.8 percent” in the three months through June 30, said chief executive Hilton Schlosberg on the company’s earnings call on August 6. The growth is remarkable given Monster’s age — it was founded in 2002 — and the challenges faced by upstart rivals like Celsius in this market. (The latter brand’s revenue declined almost 12 percent on the quarter, though it was buoyed by strong performance from Alani Nu, which it acquired in 2025.) And of course, there’s the “Trump trade war” of it all to contend with, though Schlosberg told analysts he didn’t expect Monster to experience much harm from the tariffs beyond “a continued modest sequential increase in our aluminum costs through at least the end of 2026.” Yes, things are going very well indeed for Monster Beverage Corporation these days, and it has the $90-billion market capitalization to show for it.

Of course, this is a beer column, and as such, you will likely have noticed that Monster’s CEO conspicuously carved out Monster Brewing Company from these top-line results. “Excluding the alcohol brand segment from our reported results is purely illustrative as it remains part of our ongoing operations,” Schlosberg said. Which is a bit of an issue, because while MBC is raking in the chips, its bev-alc division is crapping out faster than Tim Robinson in a toupee.

Through the second quarter of the year, Monster Brewing posted a year-over-year net sales decrease of 15.2 percent, or $32.2 million. Not to put too fine a point on it, but that’s bad compared to both the overall beer business, and the craft brewing segment, neither of which are doing particularly well at the moment. It’s even bad compared to the division’s own first-quarter performance, when it managed to eke out a net sales loss of just 5.9 percent. The World Cup, which really hit its programming stride once the knockout round began just days before the end of Q2 on June 28, delivered very mixed results for the category, as Hop Take has previously reported. By the looks of off-premise scans, at least, the stretch since the quarter’s close has been a real mixed bag for Monster Brewing, too.

The CANarchy Craft Brewery Collective — the network of half a dozen craft-beer brands that MBC acquired in 2022 for $330 million to jumpstart its bev-alc ambitions — has actually performed decently well in multi-outlet grocery, mass retail, and convenience stores tracked by the market-research firm Circana, posting mid-to-low single-digit percentages on dollar growth and just-barely there volume growth in two consecutive 30-day frames through mid-August. This is hardly gangbusters stuff, but it’s outpacing the category, which was slightly in the red on both measures for both periods. Cigar City’s Jai Alai, the closest thing Monster Brewing has to a company-wide beer flagship, is up 6.3 percent in dollars and 2.5 percent in volume year-to-date through August 9 — a darn solid result in this market, even if that growth has decelerated a bit in the most recent four weeks.

The portfolio formerly known as CANarchy is meaningfully larger than Monster Brewing’s “everything else” bucket, which is led by its Beast Unleashed flavored malt beverage. But the point of MBC’s nine-figure buy-in nearly five years ago was to set up the beverage juggernaut with a turnkey “platform” of production infrastructure, routes to market, and so forth that would allow it to quickly transmogrify its energy-drink marketing prowess into drink-drink revenues with new brands that could fill niches out of reach to traditional brewers.

This was sound logic, and it continues to be, what with virtually all the bev-alc growth opportunities coming from the flavor-forward meta-segment. The top 10 vendors in beer, wine, and spirits — 27 companies in total, because a few overlap — grew NIQ-tracked off-premise dollars of what Bump Williams Consulting calls “flavored alcohol” by 31.4 percent over the 52 weeks through June 6, compared to the same period in 2022. That figure, calculated by the longtime trade consultancy and first reported by Brewbound earlier this month, overshadows the moderating growth year-over-year between 2025 and 2026, when the cohort — larded with entries from new brands and cannibalizing extensions from existing firms — was up 3.3 percent. But that’s still better than those vendors’ “traditional” sales last year, which were down 3.3 percent in dollars.

The thing is, despite its tastebud-pwning pedigree, Monster Brewing has not figured out how to ride the flavor wave. After showing some early promise, The Beast Unleashed has struggled mightily to find a dedicated, scaled consumer base. Its rollout this year of Perfect 10, a 10-percent alcohol-by-volume tallboy primed to compete with the Twisted Tea Extremes and White Claw Surges of the gas-station fridge, came and went with nary a whisper. MBC understands the convenience-store channel’s thirsty customer about as well as any firm in the country, but its non-beer offerings have been getting clobbered. Monster Brewing LLC (under which Circana buckets all the company’s beyond-beer stuff) is down 21.9 percent in dollars and 23.7 in volume year-to-date in the latest scan sheet. What’s worse: those losses are accelerating in the most recent four-week period. The Beast Unleashed does not have a meaningful on-premise footprint. For the foreseeable future, the c-store is the ballgame, and Monster Brewing is losing it.

This raises two questions. The first is: what gives? How did MBC, with a sophisticated marketing operation mind-melded to the American manosphere’s drywall-punching id and visions of bev-alc grandeur, wind up with a mid-major craft-beer business that’s substantively outperforming its new flavored brands in a market that’s down on craft and up on flavor? You can chalk some of this up to the operational vagaries of the bev-alc business. Rodney Sacks, Schlosberg’s former co-CEO, told analysts as much in January 2025 by way of explaining an upcoming impairment charge MBC was then planning to take on the brewing division. (It was a doozy, bringing the company’s total bev-alc write-downs to $181.5 million in March 2025; that number soared in March 2026 to $232.4 million, or roughly 70 percent of the original purchase price.)

There’s also the gaping hole in Monster Brewing’s portfolio where a spirits-based ready-to-drink offering should be. As consumers have shifted to that format, major bev-alc firms from Anheuser-Busch InBev to the Mark Anthony Group have acquired brands to follow that spending. Even Molson Coors made an M&A move in that direction, acquiring Monaco Cocktails earlier this year. That’s the way the wind is blowing, especially in the c-store, where loosening rules around placements have allowed spirits-based stuff more market access. Monster Brewing is missing out on that entire market.

This brings us to the second question, which is in dialogue with the first: how much does this matter? For a company like, say, Tilray Brands, its bev-alc division matters a lot, especially since federal legalization of recreational marijuana use remains such a quagmire. The Canadian conglomerate’s dozens of craft breweries are “one of Tilray’s most important growth engines,” as CEO Irwin Simon put it on an earnings call last month. That’s just not true for MBC. With the overall company firing on all cylinders and racking up serious net-sales growth from its core business, its brewing division doesn’t have to stir its own drink. Whether this has engendered a lack of urgency within Monster Brewing is impossible to say from the outside looking in. (If you’d like to tell me about it, get in touch: dave@dinfontay.com. Anonymity available.) For now, it’s playing with house money in a sense.

Of course, MBC is a publicly traded company, not a casino. And at some point, the house money usually runs out. When the day comes for Monster Brewing to roll the dice for its own dinner, will it come up big, or go bust? If I had to place a bet today, I know which one I’d stack my chips behind. But for now, the game goes on.

🤯 Hop-ocalypse Now

Last week, the Washington Examiner published an “exclusive” report on a poll that purported to show that 65 percent of likely voters would back tariffs on Mexican beer, with 89 percent “support[ing] policies that protect American beer jobs and businesses.” This is good fodder for the Teamsters, who have been angling to get the Trump administration to make Modelo’s supply-chain costs expensive enough for parent company Constellation Brands that it decides to bring those brewing jobs north of the border. Whatever merit that scheme has, though, this data has less: it was produced by John McLaughlin, a pollster so MAGA-brained that the national Republican Party at one point warned its candidates against relying on his work.

📈 Ups…

Speaking of Constellation’s intra-continental route to market, its beer division just hired a new chief supply chain officer… Allagash Brewing Co. has a new national sales director… Tune in to your humble Hop Take columnist on recent episodes of The Brewbound Podcast and North Catch… Ninkasi Brewing acquired some $400,000 worth of Rogue Ales & Spirits barrel inventory at auction…

📉 …and downs

Sapporo USA plans to lay off 220 workers as it closes down former Stone Brewing locations in Southern California… The Brewers Association is bidding farewell to its state government affairs director…

content:
Mount Etna’s recent eruption reminded the world just how powerful volcanoes can be. For wine lovers, lava flow isn’t something to fear; rather, it’s celebrated as the source of compelling terroir. And while Etna, even when not exploding, often steals the spotlight, other regions around the world boast these unique soils.

“Volcanic wines” is an umbrella term for wines made from highly complex and varied soils originating from those fiery, smoking craters. During explosions, different volcanoes emit different types of lava, with varying levels of silicon dioxide. Along the way, the outflow picks up and moves other matter down hillsides and into valleys, creating unique layers of soil, all of which contribute to standout wines. It’s challenging terroir to farm, given the often hot, rugged terrain. In the case of Etna, you have to be somewhat of an adrenaline junkie to want to work in proximity to an active volcano, day in and day out.

But on the plus side, volcanic soils are inhospitable to pests and disease, which makes organic farming easier than in many other regions. The soils have also preserved old indigenous grape varieties. Trademark styles of volcanic wines include high acidity, salinity, and nuanced savory — rather than fruit — flavors in the forefront.

Some wine regions that benefit from volcanic soils are no longer home to active volcanoes, but still boast the complex, layered soils from eruptions of the past. Here are seven other volcanic regions beyond Mount Etna to know for wine.

Soave, Italy

Sixty-five million years ago, Soave was underwater. But subterranean explosions in fissures where the African plate had collided with the Eurasian plate created volcanoes. Over millions of years, the explosions started filling in the lagoon where Soave now stands. Volcanoes haven’t been active for 25 million years, but you can still taste the imprint on the wines. Garganega is the main grape here, although Trebbiano di Soave and Chardonnay sometimes make their way into blends. Like Chardonnay, Garganega is a fairly neutral grape that does a great job of expressing terroir. Orchard fruit, high acidity, and a through-line of acidity shine in the best wines. Producers to try: Suavia, Inama, and Pieropan.

Santorini, Greece

The island is due for a big eruption in the next 20 years, said Yiannis Paraskevopoulos of Gaia Wines in 2023. Located in what’s called the Hellenic Volcanic Arc, Santorini sits in one of the most volcanically active areas in the world. That hasn’t stopped the tourists from coming, however — or winemakers from tending to their centuries-old vines. Because of the dry and windy climate, vines are often trained in a basket shape, low to the ground. This protects vines from flying debris and breakage. The lack of disease pressure makes it possible to find vines over 200 years old. When it comes to wine, the island is best known for the zippy, mineral-driven white variety Assyrtiko. While it’s grown elsewhere in Greece, no other region matches the depth of flavor, concentration, and acidity of Santorini. Producers to try: Gaia Wines, Domaine Sigalas, and Estate Argyros.

Canary Islands, Spain

Volcanoes played a major role in developing the Canary Islands’ wine industry. On the one hand, volcanic explosions, such as a major one in Tenerife in 1706, closed ports and stunted trade. But at the same time, being closed off from international influence allowed native grapes to flourish. And given that phylloxera never made an entrance, old-vine varieties like Listán Blanco and Listán Negro found a new generation of fans when intrepid winemakers started revitalizing the industry in the 1980s and 1990s. Lanzarote, another island in the archipelago, is also defined by its rocky, black volcanic terrain. Viticulture here can be pretty challenging: The intense heat and winds make the typical vine training patterns impossible, so producers here hand-dig individual holes in the ground called “hoyos” for each of the vines, protecting each one with a small rock wall around the edges. The Producers to try: Bodegas Los Bermejos, Bodega Matías i Torres, and Bodegas Viñátigo.

Tokaj, Hungary

Active volcanoes millions of years ago left their mark on the Hungarian landscape. While the tension and minerality from the soils can be felt throughout the country’s dry reds and whites, it adds a new dimension to one of the world’s most famous sweet wines: Tokaji Aszú. Botrytis develops from the nighttime fog that blankets vineyards, transforming Furmint, Hárslevelú, and Yellow Muscat grapes into shriveled, sweetened orbs. As John Szabo notes in his book, “Volcanic Wines,” some producers believe the soils, with their mineral content, protect the vines from nefarious rot, much as salt preserves food. Taste-wise, the savory, saline qualities give these sweet wines an edginess that elevates them above other sweet wines. Producers to try: Royal Tokaji and Oremus.

Willamette Valley, Ore.

Much of the Willamette Valley soil conversation centers around marine sedimentary soils, particularly in AVAs such as Yamhill-Carlton and Ribbon Ridge, but it’s only half the story. Volcanic Jory soil — known for its red color and well-draining properties — dominate in the Dundee Hills, Eola-Amity Hills, and Chehalem Mountains AVAs. (Jory soil was actually named the state soil of Oregon in 2011.) In general, volcanic soils give more red fruit qualities to Willamette’s iconic Pinot Noirs, while marine sediment offers a darker fruit expression. Producers to try: Evening Land, Bergström Wines, 00 Wines, and CHO Wines.

Auvergne, France

For a long time, the famous beverage in Auvergne was water — Vichy water from the namesake town’s natural springs, to be specific. But in recent years, a coterie of natural winemakers sprung up in this volcanic region in central France. As mentioned before, volcanic soils favorably aid organic viticulture and, by extension, low-intervention winemaking. The grape garnering the most attention is Gamay d’Auvergne, which yields darker and spicier wines than other Gamays in France. Producers to try: Marie and Vincent Tricot, Verdier-Logel, and Henri Chauvet.

Lake County, Calif.

The Lake County AVA, located north of Napa and Sonoma, boasts some of the highest elevation vineyards in California, with the dormant Mt. Konocti volcano and other mountains defining the terrain. The volcanic soils, along with large diurnal shifts and high UV exposure, produce red wines with grippy tannins, ample acidity, and a ton of body. Cabernet Sauvignon is the signature red variety, but a whole cornucopia of other varieties, including Zinfandel, Mourvèdre, Grenache, and Petite Sirah thrive in the altitudinous vineyards. Producers to try: Obsidian Ridge Wine Co., Brassfield Estate, and Six Sigma.

content:
When chefs scan a menu at an unfamiliar spot, they approach it a bit differently than even the most discerning diner. Using their years of experience wielding a knife and vast knowledge of various ingredients, chefs are looking for small details that signal the kitchen is full of competent cooks.

Sometimes an option sticks out for using produce that’s currently at peak season or showcasing an uncommon ingredient. Other times it’s seeing a beloved, all-time favorite dish expertly prepared. So we asked eight chefs from across the country: What’s one dish you see on a menu that indicates a restaurant is worth its salt? From highly technical recipes to simply prepared, ingredient-driven plates, here are the dishes chefs see as a green flag.

The biggest green flag dishes, according to chefs:

  • Seasonally sourced seafood
  • Spaghetti al pomodoro
  • Rice
  • Roast chicken
  • Seasonal vegetables
  • Cappelletti in brodo
  • Gumbo
  • Baked oysters

“For me, it’s a green flag when a chef recognizes that seafood has seasons, too — that certain fish and shellfish are simply best at specific times of year. If they have head-on spot prawns on the menu when they’re in season, or black cod in the fall, there’s intention behind that and it demonstrates how they approach the entire menu. Source thoughtfully, pay attention to what’s at its peak, don’t intervene too much, let great ingredients lead the way.” —Esperanza Guzman, executive chef, Skaneateles Fields Resort & Spa, Skaneateles, N.Y.

“One of the biggest green flags is probably one of the simplest dishes you can make: spaghetti al pomodoro. I always think that the simpler the dish is, the more you understand about the kitchen. When you only have a few ingredients, there’s nowhere to hide. You can immediately taste the quality of the tomatoes and the olive oil, but you can also understand the technique behind the dish. How the pasta is cooked, the seasoning, the emulsification, the balance of acidity, and, most importantly, the timing. If a chef can take something as simple as spaghetti al pomodoro and make it explode with flavor, that tells me a lot.” —Pasquale Cozzolino, owner and executive chef, Ribalta, New York City

“For me, it’s rice. Nearly every culture has a defining rice dish: biryani, jollof, congee, risotto, paella, jambalaya, sushi. For thousands of years, rice has been at the center of meals, celebrations, and hospitality around the world. That’s why I pay attention to it. Rice is deceptively simple, but it demands precision and consistency. Every grain matters. Whether it’s the seasoning, moisture, texture, or temperature, there’s nowhere to hide. When a kitchen gives that level of care to something so fundamental, it’s usually a sign they’ll treat every other ingredient with the same respect.” —Ashwin Vilkhu, executive chef, The Kingsway, New Orleans

“For me, it’s a beautifully roasted chicken. It sounds simple, but there’s nowhere to hide. The skin should be deeply golden and crisp, the breast perfectly juicy, the legs fully cooked without being dry, and the sauce should be rich and glossy, built from the bird’s own juices rather than relying on butter or cream to do all the work. Every component has to be executed with precision. Any kitchen can make an elaborate dish with expensive ingredients, but a great roast chicken reveals restraint, consistency, and an understanding of the fundamentals. If a chef can make something that simple and unforgettable, it’s usually a sign the rest of the menu is in very good hands.” —Jonas Offenbach, executive chef, Serre, Hudson, N.Y.

“What I’m really looking for is a dish that shows the kitchen understands what it wants to be and is confident enough not to overwork a great ingredient. For me, a real green flag is seeing a vegetable treated with the same intention as a piece of meat or fish. When something is in season, cooked properly, seasoned with enough acid and fat to make it come alive, and doesn’t have six unnecessary things on the plate, it tells me a lot about the chef and the kitchen.” —Kyle Knall, co-owner and chef, Birch and CASSIS, Milwaukee

“For us, seeing cappelletti on a menu is a green flag because it’s a dish that showcases the fundamentals of Italian cooking. It may look simple, but there’s a lot of technique behind it: handmade pasta, a carefully prepared filling that’s cooked low and slow, and a beautiful chicken broth. Broths and sauces were some of the first things we learned to make in culinary school, so they’re foundational to how we cook. When a kitchen can execute something as seemingly simple as cappelletti with precision, balance, and depth of flavor, you know they understand the fundamentals. And beyond technique, it’s a dish rooted in tradition that brings us back to memories of Christmas and Easter.” —Andy Ticer, owner and chef, Enjoy A|M Hospitality Group (Josephine Estelle, Andrew Michael Italian Kitchen, Hog and Hominy) Memphis, Tenn.

“I know gumbo may seem simple, but several important steps are required to make a great one. Cooking the roux to achieve its deep, dark color without burning the flour is the most technical part of the process. Gumbo isn’t supposed to be spicy; it’s meant to be rich in flavor. Toasting the spices creates a balanced depth that allows the seafood to truly shine.” —Bill Briand, partner and executive chef, little bird, Fairhope, Ala.

“Baked oysters because the filling and the sourcing are a really good tell of the overall kitchen experience. You can immediately gauge when there’s good execution based on the doneness of the oyster (the texture, which is a tough thing to pull off, because it’s easy to undercook and overcook). It should have a nice texture similar to a poached egg, where it’s runny in the middle and set on the outside. Sourcing is a good tell, because it shows whether they care enough to know and thoughtfully source based on that specific product (a.k.a. knowing each type of oyster well enough to be able to make a good dish from it, and they’re proud of presenting it that way).” —David Mitchell, chef in residence, Songbird,  Raleigh, N.C.

content:
The red blend is a hallmark of Bordeaux, where it’s unusual to find single-varietal wines. Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, and a couple of minor players are almost always blended, with the emphasis guided by whether the wine is from the Left Bank (Cabernet Sauvignon) or Right Bank (Merlot).

In the United States, by contrast, red blends aren’t as strictly defined, but there’s a great deal to explore. One region where they are common yet relatively unheralded is New York’s Finger Lakes, where a sampling of almost 20 of the wines I tasted from different producers shows their depth, individuality, and value.

There are all kinds of variations in the Finger Lakes wines: Some are dominated by Cabernet Sauvignon, some by Merlot, and some by Cabernet Franc, which many consider the region’s top red variety. Still other blends include non-Bordeaux reds such as Lemberger (also called Blaufränkisch) and Saperavi, the inky red variety native to the country of Georgia.

Finger Lakes reds reflect the region’s cooler climate. They’ve got plenty of acidity and lower alcohol levels, often in the 12 to 13 percent range, which makes them excellent food wines. The style evokes the wines of another time and another place — leaner California or Bordeaux reds from the ’80s and ’90s, before the shift to power over poise in red wine, driven by a warming climate and the preferences of certain critics.

When the grapes are combined in these Finger Lakes red blends, the sum becomes much stronger than the individual varieties. With their elegance and balance, the cool-climate reds of the Finger Lakes offer a fresh perspective on the American red blend, and should definitely be on your radar.

Here are 11 of the best red blends from the Finger Lakes:

Lakewood Vineyards Sixty/40 2024

This blend of 60 percent Cabernet Sauvignon and 40 percent Cab Franc opens up to reveal ripe cherry and raspberry notes and touches of vanilla and herbs. The concentrated fruit has a leafy touch characteristic of Cab Franc. The wine was aged for 14 months in French oak barrels, but the wood influence is minimal. This fruity, high-acid blend of Cabernet Franc and Merlot — the winery calls it a tribute to the famed Château Cheval Blanc in Saint-Émilion — is simply delicious with its red berry and blueberry aromas and flavors and its mineral and earth notes. This wine drinks like a young Bordeaux and will come into its own in the next several years. Almost half the blend is Petit Verdot, which gives the wine its deep color. This wine from Seneca Lake mirrors a Right Bank Bordeaux blend, with 70 percent Merlot and 30 percent Cabernet Sauvignon. content:
What happens when “Euro summer” meets “island time?” The two laid-back, beachy vibes meet in liquid form in Italy’s island liqueurs. Off the coast of the boot, Italy has hundreds of islands from large to small, scattered across the Mediterranean. Similar to the cultural centers across the mainland, many of them produce their own beverages by sourcing local ingredients and steeping them in neutral alcohols. Tasting through these liqueurs can give consumers a glimpse of the islands’ terroirs.

Aperitifs like Aperol might dominate the Italian — and global — cocktail scene right now, but the islands offer a suite of regional products, from local amari to botanical liqueurs that showcase local fruits and flowers. While they can get the Spritz treatment, we encourage the liqueur-curious to sip these spirits straight, just as locals would.

From the scenic lemon groves off of the Amalfi Coast to the sulfuric slopes of Sicily’s Mount Etna, here are four Italian island liqueurs to know.

Capri: Limoncello

Today, tourists across the Amalfi Coast encounter dozens of tchotchke shops full of pastel-yellow limoncello handles and shooters, but the spirit has much more traditional roots. Coming from Capri, an island off the coast where lemon groves with massive, egg-shaped fruit are plentiful, the spirit first came about in the early 20th century. It is made by steeping lemon peels in a high-proof base alcohol and mixing it with sugar and water. (The recipe is so simple that you can make it at home.) With citrus peels headlining the flavor profile, the sweet lemon liqueur can lean into bitter territory, but it can also be sessionable, depending on how much sugar and water is added. The ABV for a typical bottle falls between 25 to 32 percent. Limoncello is traditionally served ice-cold in small glasses to be slowly sipped as a digestivo.

Ischia: Rucolino

As some English-speaking countries refer to arugula as “rocket,” the word for the plant in Italian has a similar root. “Rucola” means arugula, giving the name of “Rucolino,” an arugula-based amaro from the Ischia island off the coast of Naples. The Rucolino process begins with infusing a base alcohol with arugula, citrus peel, and a mix of botanicals for around 40 days. Then, producers sweeten the liqueur with sugar or syrup before letting it age. Rucolino’s flavor retains the fresh, peppery bite of arugula with bittersweet, herbaceous undertones. Much like other amari, the liqueur is traditionally consumed as a post-meal digestivo.

Sardinia: Mirto

Mirto is a liqueur made with the berries of a myrtle plant, an evergreen shrub indigenous to the Mediterranean. Some accounts suggest Mirto’s production began in Corsica and was later transported to Sardinia, now the home base of the spirit. Many of the island’s inhabitants make batches of Mirto at home for recreational consumption, and only a few professional producers exist. Making the beverage begins with steeping the berries in a high-proof neutral alcohol for up to 60 days. They then strain the liquid, separately press the fruit, and mix in the juice, the volume depending on how much they want to proof the batch down. The ensemble then goes through a final filtration process, resulting in a dark, black currant-colored spirit. The myrtle berries impart their herbal, spicy, and almost savory taste, leading into a lingering, slightly burning finish. The traditional, berry-based Mirto is known as Mirto Rosso. The island also offers Mirto Bianco, made from the less common white variety of the myrtle berries, or the leaves of the plant.

Sicily: Amaro Averna

While Sicily’s beverage scene may be better known for the wines coming from the hot, volcanic slopes of Mount Etna, the island also offers delicious local amari. The history behind Amaro Averna isn’t entirely clear, but the brand suggests monks based in Caltanissetta passed off the original recipe to Salvatore Averna, a textile merchant, in 1868. Later generations of the family continued to build the brand, expanding its popularity worldwide, and eventually turning Fratelli Averna into a corporation in 1958. The Campari Group eventually picked it up in 2014 for €103 million ($120 million) before selling it off, along with Mirto brand Zedda Piras, for €100 million ($116 million). Despite all of the switches in ownership, Amaro Averna’s production still remains faithful to the original 19th-century recipe. The blend of botanicals is a secret, but the liqueur, bottled at 29 percent ABV, brings flavors of citrus, caramel, cola, and herbs. Sicily is also home to a few other artisanal amaro brands that work with local botanicals, including Amaro dell’Etna.

title: Two Years After American Single Malt’s Ratification, the Category Is Still Finding Its Way
summary:

They eagerly anticipated positive outcomes: more consumer recognition, smoother paths to the shelf, higher sales. content:
It’s been nearly two years since the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB) ratified a standard of identity for American single malt. The milestone was hailed as a victory by distillers across the country, many of whom had been petitioning the TTB for years via the American Single Malt Whiskey Commission (ASMWC). They eagerly anticipated positive outcomes: more consumer recognition, smoother paths to the shelf, higher sales.

Such hopes remain, by and large, unrealized, as the American single malt category is dealing with the same economic challenges that are depressing sales of other whiskeys. “Things are happening slower than a lot of us would like to see simply because it’s tough times out there,” says Steve Hawley, president of the AMSWC. “I wish with all my life that it didn’t take 10 years to do what we did and we had that ratification a few years earlier when boom times were still going. The timing is unfortunate but we’re not different from any other category of whiskey right now.”

A few distilleries have gone out of business, and even some of the biggest producers of American single malt are taking it on the chin. Seattle-based Westland Distillery, owned by Rémy Cointreau, lost $1 million worth of whiskey to theft last summer; although that was a matter of bad luck, the distillery also laid off multiple staff members at the beginning of the year. Diageo subsidiary Distill Ventures wound down in 2025, leading one of the distilleries in which it held a stake, Portland, Ore.’s Westward Whiskey, to file for bankruptcy. And Diageo-owned Balcones Distillery in Waco, Texas stopped production altogether in August 2025, laying off 17 staff (and with the company’s new CEO pledging significant cuts to the workforce, more layoffs wouldn’t come as a surprise).

Still, there are bright spots. News of ratification sparked interest from the media, which has drawn attention to the niche category and provided opportunities to introduce and explain it. Producers have used the official designation to push retailers and bar owners to create dedicated sections for American single malt on their shelves and menus. And whiskey aficionados who may have had questions before are now becoming dialed in to what makes American single malt distinct, especially in relation to other whiskey styles.

“We no longer get bourbon lovers coming in and saying ‘I don’t like American single malt because I don’t like peated whiskey’,” says Justin Aden, head blender at Stranahan’s, the largest American single malt brand. The misunderstanding — that American single malt would be peated, as many Scotches are — used to be common among American whiskey drinkers visiting the distillery. Aden adds that consumers also have a better understanding of the difference between a bourbon mash bill and a 100-percent malted barley whiskey. “It sounds elementary, but it was literally not on anyone’s radar before,” he says.

But what American single malt is, and what makes it distinct, remain mostly unknown outside of connoisseur circles. Even releases from major bourbon and Tennessee whiskey brands like Jim Beam, Bulleit, and Jack Daniel’s don’t seem to have moved the needle much, although Jack remains committed to style, announcing a nationwide rollout in August. “Establishing the standard was really the beginning of building the category rather than the culmination of it,” says Jason Moore, managing director at Westland. Producers aren’t giving up, but they are adapting and looking for other opportunities to establish the category, bit by bit.

Effects of Ratification

The buildup to ratification took about a decade, which sounds like a long time but was relatively quick for an agency like the TTB. The agency had gone more than 50 years without adding a new whiskey category to the books before approving the standard of identity for American single malt in December 2024. Distillers and brands were hoping that the momentum would carry over into a positive impact on sales, but few have seen that materialize.

“We had high hopes, but it’s pretty much the same struggle,” says Stephen Paul, founder of Tucson’s Whiskey Del Bac. “Bourbon is the American whiskey. That’s a tough hurdle to get over.” He notes, however, that local stores have created dedicated sections for American single malt, something the distillery has long advocated for.

The standard of identity should get some of the credit for that, Hawley says. “It helps us in some of the practical trade aspects of making and selling whiskey,” he explains, noting that it gives retailers “incentive to create a separate shelf in their store, which we’ve shown, time and time again, is critical for our producers to be able to sell it.” Official recognition by an agency of the U.S. government also helps with tasks like export reporting; before, American single malt was just lumped into the category of “other,” making it difficult to accurately track sales.

But outside of the trade, among most consumers, the standard of identity holds little meaning, and producers still have to do some amount of education about American single malt, especially as it compares to the much more familiar category of bourbon. “I do 300 educational events a year in Oregon alone. People say, ‘Oh, whiskey, that’s not bourbon.’ You have to really start from the beginning,” says Mark Stell, founder of Bird Creek, an American single malt that focuses on unique barley varieties. “They just assume whiskey is Scotch. You have to start from the basics.”

Stell adds that distribution is another key challenge for Bird Creek, as it is for many small producers. Consolidation at the middle tier, coupled with the oversaturation of brands on the retail shelf, has narrowed avenues for growth, especially in the last couple of years. “It’s a dogfight, store to store and shelf to shelf,” says Gareth Moore, CEO of Virginia Distillery Company. “We’re investing a ton in sales and marketing to have very modest growth.”

Adjusting Expectations and Strategy

As demand for American single malt has failed to keep pace with projections, distillers are responding in different ways. In Westward’s case, the bankruptcy filing allowed it to restructure and become more agile for current conditions. CEO Tom Mooney says that the brand is “bigger today than it was before bankruptcy. We actually managed to grow over the last year and a half.”

Elsewhere, single malt distillers have leaned into new products and even diversified into different spirits altogether. Virginia Distillery Company’s Courage & Conviction single malt brand, retail-priced between $80 and $120, used to make up two-thirds of sales, but Moore says that in the last couple of years its share has fallen to one-third. The balance has shifted to the distillery’s line of cask-finished single malts, which are about half the price. Moore surmises that consumers are more comfortable with trial when the initial outlay is smaller.

“We had high hopes, but it’s pretty much the same struggle. Bourbon is the American whiskey. That’s a tough hurdle to get over.”

But Virginia Distillery Company has also moved beyond just offering single malt, incorporating a subsidiary called Pound & Penny Spirits whose portfolio includes Cierto Tequila and Kinda Light Vodka Seltzer. In addition, the company recently launched The Split Barrel Project, a bourbon–single malt blend that Moore says is acting as a gateway to the other whiskeys. “Consumers like the taste and the concept as a stepping stone,” he notes. “It’s a way to get people into the category.”

Whiskey Del Bac began expanding into bourbon and rye a few years ago with its Sentinel of the Desert line, comprising bourbon and rye from MGP that’s finished with staves from the distillery’s own mesquite-smoked whiskey casks. Paul was reluctant to diversify but the move made business sense. “We always had questions: Will you ever do a rye or bourbon? We always said no because the vision was a regional American single malt,” he explains. “Then we realized that there would be a demand and, from a cost standpoint, we needed a more cocktail-friendly whiskey.”

Stranahan’s is also targeting mixology with its Blue Peak expression, a blend of 4- to 7-year-old barrels priced around $40 at retail. “We’ve seen mixologists and bartenders shocked at the versatility of it,” Aden says. “It can fool you for a bourbon or Irish whiskey in a lot of cocktails. With the price where it is, it has been a tremendous gateway to the on premise.”

Overseas Opportunity

Unsurprisingly, American single malt producers have largely focused on domestic sales, but many say that export markets present a ripe opportunity for growth — even despite the reputational damage American whiskey is suffering. One big advantage is that the category doesn’t require a preamble of explanation overseas as it does here.

“Normally in the U.S. I find we’re explaining not what we are but what we aren’t. We’re American but we’re not bourbon. We’re single malt but we’re not Scotch,” Moore says. “Then you go international and start to explain it and someone’s like, ‘No, we get it.’ Globally the taste profile for whiskey is malt. You say whiskey overseas, they think malt.” Virginia Distillery Company currently exports to countries in Asia and Europe, as well as Australia.

Exporting American single malt requires tweaking of strategy and message but producers say it’s actually easier in many ways. “It’s an entirely different selling and marketing process when you don’t have to explain the category,” Mooney says. “The consumer understands malt whiskey and you can go straight to what makes you different. You’re not category building or explaining — you’re just telling your brand story.”

Making the jump to export isn’t necessarily straightforward, though, especially in the current sociopolitical climate. Stell was recently approached by a European importer looking for American whiskey like Bird Creek but, he says, “we have an idiotic tariff situation.” He remains hopeful that he’ll be able to make it work. “If you have a decent product, there’s a call for it, no question. Overseas markets want good products and they want a range of stuff.”

Although it’s the leading producer of American single malt, Stranahan’s has focused almost exclusively on the domestic market for its 23-year history. “We’ve always had this overlying philosophy that we didn’t really want to crack the overseas market until we could come to play with double-digit age statements,” Aden says. “Because overseas, that’s what they expect.” Now that its core line includes 10- and 12-year-old whiskeys — with higher age statements to come — Stranahan’s will begin expanding into other countries over the next couple of years.

Long Runway

Even if brands find success overseas, they still need drinkers at home to embrace the category too. With whiskey of all kinds in a rough patch, there are signs that American single malt may be better positioned than many of its bourbon and rye peers. “For better or worse there was never a bubble to burst within American single malt, so there was not a precipitous fall,” Moore says. “On a very small base it continued to grow through 2025 and so that’s a good thing for us.”

But patience, and perspective, are required. Overall sales of the category are a rounding error next to the behemoth bourbon, though Aden says that “the potential that American single malt has, even if it claws just a couple percentage points of the pie, is remarkable.”

It’s a big opportunity that will take time, but can happen if drinkers come to understand and support what makes American single malt special, just as they do with bourbon. “The exciting thing now is to try to explain that you should have just as much pride in American single malt as being a unique product of our country and representing our place as you have with bourbon,” Aden says. “We’re not trying to challenge bourbon as America’s whiskey top dog. You can have both.”

Moore points to other nontraditional single malt nations as a model of what American single malt could become: well-known, respected, beloved. “If Japan can do it and India can do it,” he says, “then sure as hell we can do it.”

content:
From line cooks and expeditors to chef-owners, back-of-house employees see how a restaurant runs from the kitchen standpoint. That behind-the-scenes knowledge gives them a unique perspective and can come in handy when dining out, especially when it comes to spotting red flags in a space.

On nights out, a chef’s sense of how a restaurant is running is just as keen as their palate, and there are certain cues that instantly set off alarms. That’s why we asked cooks and operators for the biggest red flags they notice when sitting down at a restaurant. Unsurprisingly, many call out unfriendly service as a big factor in detecting shady spots, but there are some specific signs to watch out for that can be an early indicator of the quality of the meal that lies ahead.

Here are the red flags you should clock when visiting a restaurant, according to eight restaurant pros.

The biggest red flags when sitting down at a restaurant, according to chefs:

  • An unwelcoming host
  • Rushed service
  • Unhappy staff
  • Bad pacing
  • Bad energy
  • Unattentive team
  • Dirty bathroom
  • Overlooking the guest experience
  • Dirty menus
  • White wines cooled indiscriminately in an ice bucket

“Honestly, the biggest red flag can happen before I even sit down. The host stand is crucial for setting the tone of the experience. I’ve had so many interactions with hosts who seem indifferent or annoyed by my presence, which is hard to recover from. A warm, sincere greeting goes such a long way.” —John Manion, chef, El Che and Brasero, Chicago

“I instantly notice when a restaurant makes guests feel rushed, whether it is through the pace of greeting diners as they walk through the doors, the ordering process, or the speed at which courses are cleared. A good meal should have rhythm, but it should never feel like a restaurant is trying to get you in and out as fast as possible. When hospitality is rushed and not authentic, that is the biggest red flag a restaurant can have.” —Avtar Singh Walia, owner, Tamarind Tribeca, New York City

“When I’m dining in a restaurant and the staff look miserable but are plastering on a ‘happy’ face for the guest, it’s a red flag for me. Working with people always brings conflict — it’s the nature of it. But if the crew seems stuck in tension or drama, the guest-forward hospitality feels performative instead of genuine. It’s often a sign that something is off in the culture. Every customer-facing workforce experiences times like these, but the trick lies in how to move through them so we don’t get stuck there and can return to a lightness of being with each other and a work environment we all look forward to being in. The impact our internal culture has on our external hospitality is huge.” —Molly Irani, co-founder, Chai Pani Restaurant Group, author, Service Ready, Asheville, N.C.

“A big red flag when I sit down at a restaurant is timing. If the time between when I sit down, get a glass of water, and take my first bite of food is too long, I become agitated and hangry. If the time between the following courses is too long, I easily get bored — especially at a tasting menu experience, even if it’s unintentional. Overall, this could indicate a lack of service staff, attentiveness, or a sense of urgency.” —David Yoshimura, executive chef and owner, Nisei, San Francisco

“While I try to remain open-minded, there are certain things that I register. The first is the energy of the room and the people working in it: How was my party greeted? Then comes the menu: Is it clear? Then, I watch the choreography of the meal: How attentive is the team? Even the restroom tells me something: Is it clean? Ultimately, all of these observations lead me back to one question: Do I matter? Great hospitality isn’t simply about serving good food. It’s about making someone feel seen, welcomed, cared for, and genuinely valued from the moment they walk through the door until the moment they leave. The biggest red flag is when the restaurant’s priorities become obvious and the guest isn’t one of them. A restaurant can have a bad night. It can be slammed. A dish can take too long. A server can make a mistake. Those things happen. What I’m watching for is what happens around those imperfections. Do I see a team that cares, communicates, recovers, and protects the guest experience, or one that has forgotten that the guest is the reason everyone is there? That’s the red flag I notice most: Do I matter?” —Oren Cohen, general manager, The Bindery, Denver

“The biggest red flag is being handed dirty menus when I first sit down. I think that creates a very unwelcoming feeling for a guest, starting off the experience without feeling cared for. It’s hard to win a guest back after that happens!” —Charlie Mitchell, chef, Saga, NYC

“Vibes are important at a restaurant, and they can really impact your experience as a guest. Working in the industry, it’s always obvious when I sit down at a restaurant and there’s tension in the air. Happy servers and cooks — open kitchens are trending — make for better food and dining experiences. So, a big red flag for me is when staff don’t look engaged and excited, which tells me management is not creating a positive work environment.” —Chris McLaurin, chef, Lutra Cafe & Bakery, Durham, N.C.

“All the white wine indiscriminately in an ice bucket at the bar or at a service station, at least at a nicer restaurant with a pricy by-the-glass and bottle list that’s meant to impress. Properly tempered wine should be the bare minimum.” —Zach Engel, chef, Galit and Cafe Yaya, Chicago

content:
In the two decades since the Honey Deuce first debuted at the US Open, the drink has arguably become even more of a draw than the game itself. Tennis fans miss entire sets while standing in line for the cocktail, while others stack souvenir cups to show off how many combinations of Grey Goose vodka, lemonade, and raspberry liqueur they’ve consumed that afternoon.

But this year, a fresh tennis-themed drink is vying to dethrone the tournament’s defending champion at the bar. The US Open’s newest cocktail is called the Moët Serve and it’s a simple combination of bubbles provided by Moët & Chandon, the official Champagne of the event, a squeeze of lime, and ice.

The specs might not sound like much. But served in a collectible cup that looks like a tennis ball canister with three lime wheel garnishes stacked up to resemble tennis balls, it precisely follows the formula for iconic sporting event drinks like the Honey Deuce and Pimm’s Cup so it will surely appear on your Instagram feed a lot over the next few weeks.

The drink uses Moët Ice Impérial, a bottle that was released by the brand in 2010 as the first Champagne designed to be served with ice. Clocking in with a dosage of 45 grams/liter, the bubbles fall solidly into demi-sec territory, which is typically considered quite sweet — especially compared to the brand’s flagship bottle, Moët & Chandon Brut Impérial, which uses a dosage of 7 grams/liter. The increased sugar dials up the fruity notes already present in the wine and adds sweetness that could be considered cloying in most contexts. But in this case, when the bubbles cascade over cubes of ice, the intensity levels out.

While the cocktail is by no means complex, neither is its predecessor. The Honey Deuce is a simple vodka lemonade at its core, and with most iterations using big-brand bottled lemonades, it can also be quite sugary.

Instead of going for artisanal ingredients or ambitious technique, the Honey Deuce aimed to capture the zeitgeist with a garnish of three scoops of honeydew melon that look like tennis balls perched on top of the glass, and it clearly worked. Last year, the three-week tournament sold more than 738,000 Honey Deuces and raked in $17 million, a 32 percent year-over-year increase.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Lev Akabas, Data Visualization (@datakabas)

With three lime wheels pressed up against the side of the canister-shaped cup, the Moët Serve also leans on its photo-worthy garnish, which is no-doubt compelling to a certain set of tournament goers. Plus, like the Honey Deuce, Moët’s signature drink will also be available beyond the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center grounds at select locations throughout New York City, including Dante, Electric Lemon, and The St. Regis New York.

Though the Moët Serve might be a worthy competitor, the Honey Deuce still has a clear step up in maintaining its title as the most iconic drink of the event. First of all, there’s no denying home court advantage. The US Open is clear Honey Deuce territory, and it has widened its domain beyond the court as well, so much so that it feels like most bars across NYC offer their own take on the Honey Deuce during the tournament. It’s become so much of a status symbol, it’s hard for many fans to imagine going to a match without snapping a pic of their Honey Deuce as proof they were there.

The other obstacle the Moët Serve will no doubt encounter is its lofty price tag. At $23, the Honey Deuce was already considered a splurge for attendees, but the Moët Serve will be available for $32 — a steep increase, even by stadium standards. It’s unclear how many people are willing to shell out $9 more for a newcomer, even if it is Champagne-based.

So while the Honey Deuce is entering the tournament as the top seeded drink, the Moët Serve’s simplicity and eye-catching garnish could make it the dark horse to win the major this year. Though, it’d be a real upset.

title: Monster Beverage Is Making More Money Than Its Brewing Division Can Lose
summary:
Gambling is fun. Unless you lose. Unless-unless you were gambling with house money the whole time. In which case, who cares? Hold that thought. They were pretty spectacular. “Net sales, excluding the alcohol brand segment, increased 20.8 percent” in the three months through June 30, said chief executive Hilton Schlosberg on the company’s earnings call on August 6. The growth is remarkable given Monster’s age — it was founded in 2002 — and the challenges faced by upstart rivals like Celsius in this market.

content:
Gambling is fun. Unless you lose. Unless-unless you were gambling with house money the whole time. In which case, who cares?

Hold that thought. Earlier this month, Monster Beverage Corporation (MBC) reported its earnings for the second quarter of 2026. They were pretty spectacular.

“Net sales, excluding the alcohol brand segment, increased 20.8 percent” in the three months through June 30, said chief executive Hilton Schlosberg on the company’s earnings call on August 6. The growth is remarkable given Monster’s age — it was founded in 2002 — and the challenges faced by upstart rivals like Celsius in this market. (The latter brand’s revenue declined almost 12 percent on the quarter, though it was buoyed by strong performance from Alani Nu, which it acquired in 2025.) And of course, there’s the “Trump trade war” of it all to contend with, though Schlosberg told analysts he didn’t expect Monster to experience much harm from the tariffs beyond “a continued modest sequential increase in our aluminum costs through at least the end of 2026.” Yes, things are going very well indeed for Monster Beverage Corporation these days, and it has the $90-billion market capitalization to show for it.

Of course, this is a beer column, and as such, you will likely have noticed that Monster’s CEO conspicuously carved out Monster Brewing Company from these top-line results. “Excluding the alcohol brand segment from our reported results is purely illustrative as it remains part of our ongoing operations,” Schlosberg said. Which is a bit of an issue, because while MBC is raking in the chips, its bev-alc division is crapping out faster than Tim Robinson in a toupee.

Through the second quarter of the year, Monster Brewing posted a year-over-year net sales decrease of 15.2 percent, or $32.2 million. Not to put too fine a point on it, but that’s bad compared to both the overall beer business, and the craft brewing segment, neither of which are doing particularly well at the moment. It’s even bad compared to the division’s own first-quarter performance, when it managed to eke out a net sales loss of just 5.9 percent. The World Cup, which really hit its programming stride once the knockout round began just days before the end of Q2 on June 28, delivered very mixed results for the category, as Hop Take has previously reported. By the looks of off-premise scans, at least, the stretch since the quarter’s close has been a real mixed bag for Monster Brewing, too.

The CANarchy Craft Brewery Collective — the network of half a dozen craft-beer brands that MBC acquired in 2022 for $330 million to jumpstart its bev-alc ambitions — has actually performed decently well in multi-outlet grocery, mass retail, and convenience stores tracked by the market-research firm Circana, posting mid-to-low single-digit percentages on dollar growth and just-barely there volume growth in two consecutive 30-day frames through mid-August. This is hardly gangbusters stuff, but it’s outpacing the category, which was slightly in the red on both measures for both periods. Cigar City’s Jai Alai, the closest thing Monster Brewing has to a company-wide beer flagship, is up 6.3 percent in dollars and 2.5 percent in volume year-to-date through August 9 — a darn solid result in this market, even if that growth has decelerated a bit in the most recent four weeks.

The portfolio formerly known as CANarchy is meaningfully larger than Monster Brewing’s “everything else” bucket, which is led by its Beast Unleashed flavored malt beverage. But the point of MBC’s nine-figure buy-in nearly five years ago was to set up the beverage juggernaut with a turnkey “platform” of production infrastructure, routes to market, and so forth that would allow it to quickly transmogrify its energy-drink marketing prowess into drink-drink revenues with new brands that could fill niches out of reach to traditional brewers.

This was sound logic, and it continues to be, what with virtually all the bev-alc growth opportunities coming from the flavor-forward meta-segment. The top 10 vendors in beer, wine, and spirits — 27 companies in total, because a few overlap — grew NIQ-tracked off-premise dollars of what Bump Williams Consulting calls “flavored alcohol” by 31.4 percent over the 52 weeks through June 6, compared to the same period in 2022. That figure, calculated by the longtime trade consultancy and first reported by Brewbound earlier this month, overshadows the moderating growth year-over-year between 2025 and 2026, when the cohort — larded with entries from new brands and cannibalizing extensions from existing firms — was up 3.3 percent. But that’s still better than those vendors’ “traditional” sales last year, which were down 3.3 percent in dollars.

The thing is, despite its tastebud-pwning pedigree, Monster Brewing has not figured out how to ride the flavor wave. After showing some early promise, The Beast Unleashed has struggled mightily to find a dedicated, scaled consumer base. Its rollout this year of Perfect 10, a 10-percent alcohol-by-volume tallboy primed to compete with the Twisted Tea Extremes and White Claw Surges of the gas-station fridge, came and went with nary a whisper. MBC understands the convenience-store channel’s thirsty customer about as well as any firm in the country, but its non-beer offerings have been getting clobbered. Monster Brewing LLC (under which Circana buckets all the company’s beyond-beer stuff) is down 21.9 percent in dollars and 23.7 in volume year-to-date in the latest scan sheet. What’s worse: those losses are accelerating in the most recent four-week period. The Beast Unleashed does not have a meaningful on-premise footprint. For the foreseeable future, the c-store is the ballgame, and Monster Brewing is losing it.

This raises two questions. The first is: what gives? How did MBC, with a sophisticated marketing operation mind-melded to the American manosphere’s drywall-punching id and visions of bev-alc grandeur, wind up with a mid-major craft-beer business that’s substantively outperforming its new flavored brands in a market that’s down on craft and up on flavor? You can chalk some of this up to the operational vagaries of the bev-alc business. Rodney Sacks, Schlosberg’s former co-CEO, told analysts as much in January 2025 by way of explaining an upcoming impairment charge MBC was then planning to take on the brewing division. (It was a doozy, bringing the company’s total bev-alc write-downs to $181.5 million in March 2025; that number soared in March 2026 to $232.4 million, or roughly 70 percent of the original purchase price.)

There’s also the gaping hole in Monster Brewing’s portfolio where a spirits-based ready-to-drink offering should be. As consumers have shifted to that format, major bev-alc firms from Anheuser-Busch InBev to the Mark Anthony Group have acquired brands to follow that spending. Even Molson Coors made an M&A move in that direction, acquiring Monaco Cocktails earlier this year. That’s the way the wind is blowing, especially in the c-store, where loosening rules around placements have allowed spirits-based stuff more market access. Monster Brewing is missing out on that entire market.

This brings us to the second question, which is in dialogue with the first: how much does this matter? For a company like, say, Tilray Brands, its bev-alc division matters a lot, especially since federal legalization of recreational marijuana use remains such a quagmire. The Canadian conglomerate’s dozens of craft breweries are “one of Tilray’s most important growth engines,” as CEO Irwin Simon put it on an earnings call last month. That’s just not true for MBC. With the overall company firing on all cylinders and racking up serious net-sales growth from its core business, its brewing division doesn’t have to stir its own drink. Whether this has engendered a lack of urgency within Monster Brewing is impossible to say from the outside looking in. (If you’d like to tell me about it, get in touch: dave@dinfontay.com. Anonymity available.) For now, it’s playing with house money in a sense.

Of course, MBC is a publicly traded company, not a casino. And at some point, the house money usually runs out. When the day comes for Monster Brewing to roll the dice for its own dinner, will it come up big, or go bust? If I had to place a bet today, I know which one I’d stack my chips behind. But for now, the game goes on.

🤯 Hop-ocalypse Now

Last week, the Washington Examiner published an “exclusive” report on a poll that purported to show that 65 percent of likely voters would back tariffs on Mexican beer, with 89 percent “support[ing] policies that protect American beer jobs and businesses.” This is good fodder for the Teamsters, who have been angling to get the Trump administration to make Modelo’s supply-chain costs expensive enough for parent company Constellation Brands that it decides to bring those brewing jobs north of the border. Whatever merit that scheme has, though, this data has less: it was produced by John McLaughlin, a pollster so MAGA-brained that the national Republican Party at one point warned its candidates against relying on his work.

📈 Ups…

Speaking of Constellation’s intra-continental route to market, its beer division just hired a new chief supply chain officer… Allagash Brewing Co. has a new national sales director… Tune in to your humble Hop Take columnist on recent episodes of The Brewbound Podcast and North Catch… Ninkasi Brewing acquired some $400,000 worth of Rogue Ales & Spirits barrel inventory at auction…

📉 …and downs

Sapporo USA plans to lay off 220 workers as it closes down former Stone Brewing locations in Southern California… The Brewers Association is bidding farewell to its state government affairs director…

Mount Etna’s recent eruption reminded the world just how powerful volcanoes can be. For wine lovers, lava flow isn’t something to fear; rather, it’s celebrated as the source of compelling terroir. content:
Mount Etna’s recent eruption reminded the world just how powerful volcanoes can be. For wine lovers, lava flow isn’t something to fear; rather, it’s celebrated as the source of compelling terroir. And while Etna, even when not exploding, often steals the spotlight, other regions around the world boast these unique soils.

“Volcanic wines” is an umbrella term for wines made from highly complex and varied soils originating from those fiery, smoking craters. During explosions, different volcanoes emit different types of lava, with varying levels of silicon dioxide. Along the way, the outflow picks up and moves other matter down hillsides and into valleys, creating unique layers of soil, all of which contribute to standout wines. It’s challenging terroir to farm, given the often hot, rugged terrain. In the case of Etna, you have to be somewhat of an adrenaline junkie to want to work in proximity to an active volcano, day in and day out.

But on the plus side, volcanic soils are inhospitable to pests and disease, which makes organic farming easier than in many other regions. The soils have also preserved old indigenous grape varieties. Trademark styles of volcanic wines include high acidity, salinity, and nuanced savory — rather than fruit — flavors in the forefront.

Some wine regions that benefit from volcanic soils are no longer home to active volcanoes, but still boast the complex, layered soils from eruptions of the past. Here are seven other volcanic regions beyond Mount Etna to know for wine.

Soave, Italy

Sixty-five million years ago, Soave was underwater. But subterranean explosions in fissures where the African plate had collided with the Eurasian plate created volcanoes. Over millions of years, the explosions started filling in the lagoon where Soave now stands. Volcanoes haven’t been active for 25 million years, but you can still taste the imprint on the wines. Garganega is the main grape here, although Trebbiano di Soave and Chardonnay sometimes make their way into blends. Like Chardonnay, Garganega is a fairly neutral grape that does a great job of expressing terroir. Orchard fruit, high acidity, and a through-line of acidity shine in the best wines. Producers to try: Suavia, Inama, and Pieropan.

Santorini, Greece

The island is due for a big eruption in the next 20 years, said Yiannis Paraskevopoulos of Gaia Wines in 2023. Located in what’s called the Hellenic Volcanic Arc, Santorini sits in one of the most volcanically active areas in the world. That hasn’t stopped the tourists from coming, however — or winemakers from tending to their centuries-old vines. Because of the dry and windy climate, vines are often trained in a basket shape, low to the ground. This protects vines from flying debris and breakage. The lack of disease pressure makes it possible to find vines over 200 years old. When it comes to wine, the island is best known for the zippy, mineral-driven white variety Assyrtiko. While it’s grown elsewhere in Greece, no other region matches the depth of flavor, concentration, and acidity of Santorini. Producers to try: Gaia Wines, Domaine Sigalas, and Estate Argyros.

Canary Islands, Spain

Volcanoes played a major role in developing the Canary Islands’ wine industry. On the one hand, volcanic explosions, such as a major one in Tenerife in 1706, closed ports and stunted trade. But at the same time, being closed off from international influence allowed native grapes to flourish. And given that phylloxera never made an entrance, old-vine varieties like Listán Blanco and Listán Negro found a new generation of fans when intrepid winemakers started revitalizing the industry in the 1980s and 1990s. Lanzarote, another island in the archipelago, is also defined by its rocky, black volcanic terrain. Viticulture here can be pretty challenging: The intense heat and winds make the typical vine training patterns impossible, so producers here hand-dig individual holes in the ground called “hoyos” for each of the vines, protecting each one with a small rock wall around the edges. The Producers to try: Bodegas Los Bermejos, Bodega Matías i Torres, and Bodegas Viñátigo.

Tokaj, Hungary

Active volcanoes millions of years ago left their mark on the Hungarian landscape. While the tension and minerality from the soils can be felt throughout the country’s dry reds and whites, it adds a new dimension to one of the world’s most famous sweet wines: Tokaji Aszú. Botrytis develops from the nighttime fog that blankets vineyards, transforming Furmint, Hárslevelú, and Yellow Muscat grapes into shriveled, sweetened orbs. As John Szabo notes in his book, “Volcanic Wines,” some producers believe the soils, with their mineral content, protect the vines from nefarious rot, much as salt preserves food. Taste-wise, the savory, saline qualities give these sweet wines an edginess that elevates them above other sweet wines. Producers to try: Royal Tokaji and Oremus.

Willamette Valley, Ore.

Much of the Willamette Valley soil conversation centers around marine sedimentary soils, particularly in AVAs such as Yamhill-Carlton and Ribbon Ridge, but it’s only half the story. Volcanic Jory soil — known for its red color and well-draining properties — dominate in the Dundee Hills, Eola-Amity Hills, and Chehalem Mountains AVAs. (Jory soil was actually named the state soil of Oregon in 2011.) In general, volcanic soils give more red fruit qualities to Willamette’s iconic Pinot Noirs, while marine sediment offers a darker fruit expression. Producers to try: Evening Land, Bergström Wines, 00 Wines, and CHO Wines.

Auvergne, France

For a long time, the famous beverage in Auvergne was water — Vichy water from the namesake town’s natural springs, to be specific. But in recent years, a coterie of natural winemakers sprung up in this volcanic region in central France. As mentioned before, volcanic soils favorably aid organic viticulture and, by extension, low-intervention winemaking. The grape garnering the most attention is Gamay d’Auvergne, which yields darker and spicier wines than other Gamays in France. Producers to try: Marie and Vincent Tricot, Verdier-Logel, and Henri Chauvet.

Lake County, Calif.

The Lake County AVA, located north of Napa and Sonoma, boasts some of the highest elevation vineyards in California, with the dormant Mt. Konocti volcano and other mountains defining the terrain. The volcanic soils, along with large diurnal shifts and high UV exposure, produce red wines with grippy tannins, ample acidity, and a ton of body. Cabernet Sauvignon is the signature red variety, but a whole cornucopia of other varieties, including Zinfandel, Mourvèdre, Grenache, and Petite Sirah thrive in the altitudinous vineyards. Producers to try: Obsidian Ridge Wine Co., Brassfield Estate, and Six Sigma.

content:
When chefs scan a menu at an unfamiliar spot, they approach it a bit differently than even the most discerning diner. Using their years of experience wielding a knife and vast knowledge of various ingredients, chefs are looking for small details that signal the kitchen is full of competent cooks.

Sometimes an option sticks out for using produce that’s currently at peak season or showcasing an uncommon ingredient. Other times it’s seeing a beloved, all-time favorite dish expertly prepared. So we asked eight chefs from across the country: What’s one dish you see on a menu that indicates a restaurant is worth its salt? From highly technical recipes to simply prepared, ingredient-driven plates, here are the dishes chefs see as a green flag.

The biggest green flag dishes, according to chefs:

  • Seasonally sourced seafood
  • Spaghetti al pomodoro
  • Rice
  • Roast chicken
  • Seasonal vegetables
  • Cappelletti in brodo
  • Gumbo
  • Baked oysters

“For me, it’s a green flag when a chef recognizes that seafood has seasons, too — that certain fish and shellfish are simply best at specific times of year. If they have head-on spot prawns on the menu when they’re in season, or black cod in the fall, there’s intention behind that and it demonstrates how they approach the entire menu. Source thoughtfully, pay attention to what’s at its peak, don’t intervene too much, let great ingredients lead the way.” —Esperanza Guzman, executive chef, Skaneateles Fields Resort & Spa, Skaneateles, N.Y.

“One of the biggest green flags is probably one of the simplest dishes you can make: spaghetti al pomodoro. I always think that the simpler the dish is, the more you understand about the kitchen. When you only have a few ingredients, there’s nowhere to hide. You can immediately taste the quality of the tomatoes and the olive oil, but you can also understand the technique behind the dish. How the pasta is cooked, the seasoning, the emulsification, the balance of acidity, and, most importantly, the timing. If a chef can take something as simple as spaghetti al pomodoro and make it explode with flavor, that tells me a lot.” —Pasquale Cozzolino, owner and executive chef, Ribalta, New York City

“For me, it’s rice. Nearly every culture has a defining rice dish: biryani, jollof, congee, risotto, paella, jambalaya, sushi. For thousands of years, rice has been at the center of meals, celebrations, and hospitality around the world. That’s why I pay attention to it. Rice is deceptively simple, but it demands precision and consistency. Every grain matters. Whether it’s the seasoning, moisture, texture, or temperature, there’s nowhere to hide. When a kitchen gives that level of care to something so fundamental, it’s usually a sign they’ll treat every other ingredient with the same respect.” —Ashwin Vilkhu, executive chef, The Kingsway, New Orleans

“For me, it’s a beautifully roasted chicken. It sounds simple, but there’s nowhere to hide. The skin should be deeply golden and crisp, the breast perfectly juicy, the legs fully cooked without being dry, and the sauce should be rich and glossy, built from the bird’s own juices rather than relying on butter or cream to do all the work. Every component has to be executed with precision. Any kitchen can make an elaborate dish with expensive ingredients, but a great roast chicken reveals restraint, consistency, and an understanding of the fundamentals. If a chef can make something that simple and unforgettable, it’s usually a sign the rest of the menu is in very good hands.” —Jonas Offenbach, executive chef, Serre, Hudson, N.Y.

“What I’m really looking for is a dish that shows the kitchen understands what it wants to be and is confident enough not to overwork a great ingredient. For me, a real green flag is seeing a vegetable treated with the same intention as a piece of meat or fish. When something is in season, cooked properly, seasoned with enough acid and fat to make it come alive, and doesn’t have six unnecessary things on the plate, it tells me a lot about the chef and the kitchen.” —Kyle Knall, co-owner and chef, Birch and CASSIS, Milwaukee

“For us, seeing cappelletti on a menu is a green flag because it’s a dish that showcases the fundamentals of Italian cooking. It may look simple, but there’s a lot of technique behind it: handmade pasta, a carefully prepared filling that’s cooked low and slow, and a beautiful chicken broth. Broths and sauces were some of the first things we learned to make in culinary school, so they’re foundational to how we cook. When a kitchen can execute something as seemingly simple as cappelletti with precision, balance, and depth of flavor, you know they understand the fundamentals. And beyond technique, it’s a dish rooted in tradition that brings us back to memories of Christmas and Easter.” —Andy Ticer, owner and chef, Enjoy A|M Hospitality Group (Josephine Estelle, Andrew Michael Italian Kitchen, Hog and Hominy) Memphis, Tenn.

“I know gumbo may seem simple, but several important steps are required to make a great one. Cooking the roux to achieve its deep, dark color without burning the flour is the most technical part of the process. Gumbo isn’t supposed to be spicy; it’s meant to be rich in flavor. Toasting the spices creates a balanced depth that allows the seafood to truly shine.” —Bill Briand, partner and executive chef, little bird, Fairhope, Ala.

“Baked oysters because the filling and the sourcing are a really good tell of the overall kitchen experience. You can immediately gauge when there’s good execution based on the doneness of the oyster (the texture, which is a tough thing to pull off, because it’s easy to undercook and overcook). It should have a nice texture similar to a poached egg, where it’s runny in the middle and set on the outside. Sourcing is a good tell, because it shows whether they care enough to know and thoughtfully source based on that specific product (a.k.a. knowing each type of oyster well enough to be able to make a good dish from it, and they’re proud of presenting it that way).” —David Mitchell, chef in residence, Songbird,  Raleigh, N.C.
