content:
The red blend is a hallmark of Bordeaux, where it’s unusual to find single-varietal wines. Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, and a couple of minor players are almost always blended, with the emphasis guided by whether the wine is from the Left Bank (Cabernet Sauvignon) or Right Bank (Merlot).

In the United States, by contrast, red blends aren’t as strictly defined, but there’s a great deal to explore. One region where they are common yet relatively unheralded is New York’s Finger Lakes, where a sampling of almost 20 of the wines I tasted from different producers shows their depth, individuality, and value.

There are all kinds of variations in the Finger Lakes wines: Some are dominated by Cabernet Sauvignon, some by Merlot, and some by Cabernet Franc, which many consider the region’s top red variety. Still other blends include non-Bordeaux reds such as Lemberger (also called Blaufränkisch) and Saperavi, the inky red variety native to the country of Georgia.

Finger Lakes reds reflect the region’s cooler climate. They’ve got plenty of acidity and lower alcohol levels, often in the 12 to 13 percent range, which makes them excellent food wines. The style evokes the wines of another time and another place — leaner California or Bordeaux reds from the ’80s and ’90s, before the shift to power over poise in red wine, driven by a warming climate and the preferences of certain critics.

When the grapes are combined in these Finger Lakes red blends, the sum becomes much stronger than the individual varieties. With their elegance and balance, the cool-climate reds of the Finger Lakes offer a fresh perspective on the American red blend, and should definitely be on your radar.

Here are 11 of the best red blends from the Finger Lakes:

Lakewood Vineyards Sixty/40 2024

This blend of 60 percent Cabernet Sauvignon and 40 percent Cab Franc opens up to reveal ripe cherry and raspberry notes and touches of vanilla and herbs. There’s a hint of eucalyptus on the nose and a bit of the bell pepper of Cab Franc. Though it’s based on Bordeaux varieties, it came across more Pinot Noir-like in its fruit profile and mouthfeel.

Price: $40
Buy This Wine

Airy Acres Aviator’s Red 2024

Who would have thought that Lemberger (Blaufränkisch) would blend well with Cab Franc? Well, they did at this relatively new Cayuga Lake winery, and it works. The blend is roughly half and half, and the result is a wine marked by delicious red and dark fruit notes with hints of cinnamon and spice. The concentrated fruit has a leafy touch characteristic of Cab Franc. The wine was aged for 14 months in French oak barrels, but the wood influence is minimal. Lively acidity keeps it fresh, and alcohol is a moderate 12.6 percent. Also worth trying: Airy Acres’ 2023 Vinifera Red Blend, which includes some Saperavi and Cabernet Sauvignon in addition to Cab Franc and Lemerger.

Price: $22
Buy This Wine

Bloomer Creek Vineyard White Horse Red Blend 2021

This fruity, high-acid blend of Cabernet Franc and Merlot — the winery calls it a tribute to the famed Château Cheval Blanc in Saint-Émilion — is simply delicious with its red berry and blueberry aromas and flavors and its mineral and earth notes. It reminded me more of a Loire Valley Cab Franc or perhaps a Beaujolais made with carbonic maceration. A number of online retailers are selling it for around $10 or so, making it an almost unbelievable value.

Price: $11
Buy This Wine

Hosmer Winery Eden Red Blend 2024

This wine drinks like a young Bordeaux and will come into its own in the next several years. Almost half the blend is Petit Verdot, which gives the wine its deep color. Cabernet Sauvignon and Cab Franc are the rest of the mix. The wine has notes of blackberry, unsweetened chocolate, and sage framed by medium tannins.

Price: $35
Buy This Wine

Boundary Breaks The Harmonic 2023

This wine from Seneca Lake mirrors a Right Bank Bordeaux blend, with 70 percent Merlot and 30 percent Cabernet Sauvignon. It’s a softer expression that’s lightly tannic with blackberry and black cherry notes and a hint of pencil shavings. The winery says it uses early leaf removal and crop-thinning in mid-August, techniques that enable it to produce “uncommonly ripe fruit in a cool climate.”

Price: $25
Buy This Wine

Wagner Vineyards Meritage 2020

The refined blend of 45 percent Cabernet Sauvignon, 38 percent Cab Franc, and 17 percent Merlot starts off with aromas of pomegranate and raspberry, but as it opens up, darker fruit notes emerge on the palate along with touches of vanilla and spices from 12 months in American oak barrels. It’s all framed by smooth tannins and the region’s vibrant acidity.

Price: $30
Buy This Wine

Thirsty Owl Meritage 2024

This wine from Cayuga Lake is a blend of 63 percent Cabernet Sauvignon, 31 percent Cab Franc, and 6 percent Merlot. And it really pops as a refreshing food companion. Bright acidity supports cranberry and plum aromas and flavors, along with a touch of leather and a subtle vanilla overlay. Moderate tannins extend on the long finish.

Price: $29
Buy This Wine

Dr. Konstantin Frank Lena Reserve 2023

The price of this wine puts it up there with many top American reds, but it’s justified. It’s one of the more unusual blends, dominated by Blaufränkisch, Merlot, and Saperavi with smaller amounts of Cab Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon. Complex and relatively deep in color, its notes of concentrated dark fruit and violets are accented by hints of fennel and cumin seeds, earth, and a chalky minerality. Still a bit tightly wound, it’s a wine to enjoy now but it will evolve for several years. The wine is named for a daughter of the founder, Dr. Konstantin Frank. The ’22 vintage is available on the website.

Price: $60
Buy This Wine

Heron Hill The Chosen Spot Ingle Vineyard 2023

Concentrated fruit is the hallmark of this wine from Keuka Lake, with red and dark fruit notes including pomegranate, raspberry, and cassis. The blend of Cab Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Merlot has hints of bell pepper and herbs supported by a medium tannic structure. It’s aged for 19 to 20 months in French oak barrels, but the wood is well integrated.

Price: $50
Buy This Wine

Damiani Wine Cellars Meritage 2022

This elegant blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, and Cab Franc from Seneca Lake is marked by ripe red and dark fruit notes and stony minerality. Black cherry, raspberry, and fresh blueberry aromas and flavors are punctuated by vanilla and spice notes and supported by lively acidity. A lovely wine now, it will continue to develop for several more years.

Price: $45
Buy This Wine

Atwater Vineyards Symvolí 2024

This Seneca Lake wine, a blend of 57 percent Cabernet Sauvignon, 33 percent Merlot, and 10 percent Cab Franc, is relatively soft but delicious. Notes of blackberry and cassis with vanilla, spice, and espresso accents. The 2023 vintage is available on the winery’s website.

Price: $30
Buy This Wine

content:
What happens when “Euro summer” meets “island time?” The two laid-back, beachy vibes meet in liquid form in Italy’s island liqueurs. Off the coast of the boot, Italy has hundreds of islands from large to small, scattered across the Mediterranean. Similar to the cultural centers across the mainland, many of them produce their own beverages by sourcing local ingredients and steeping them in neutral alcohols. Tasting through these liqueurs can give consumers a glimpse of the islands’ terroirs.

Aperitifs like Aperol might dominate the Italian — and global — cocktail scene right now, but the islands offer a suite of regional products, from local amari to botanical liqueurs that showcase local fruits and flowers. While they can get the Spritz treatment, we encourage the liqueur-curious to sip these spirits straight, just as locals would.

From the scenic lemon groves off of the Amalfi Coast to the sulfuric slopes of Sicily’s Mount Etna, here are four Italian island liqueurs to know.

Capri: Limoncello

Today, tourists across the Amalfi Coast encounter dozens of tchotchke shops full of pastel-yellow limoncello handles and shooters, but the spirit has much more traditional roots. Coming from Capri, an island off the coast where lemon groves with massive, egg-shaped fruit are plentiful, the spirit first came about in the early 20th century. It is made by steeping lemon peels in a high-proof base alcohol and mixing it with sugar and water. (The recipe is so simple that you can make it at home.) With citrus peels headlining the flavor profile, the sweet lemon liqueur can lean into bitter territory, but it can also be sessionable, depending on how much sugar and water is added. The ABV for a typical bottle falls between 25 to 32 percent. Limoncello is traditionally served ice-cold in small glasses to be slowly sipped as a digestivo.

Ischia: Rucolino

As some English-speaking countries refer to arugula as “rocket,” the word for the plant in Italian has a similar root. “Rucola” means arugula, giving the name of “Rucolino,” an arugula-based amaro from the Ischia island off the coast of Naples. The Rucolino process begins with infusing a base alcohol with arugula, citrus peel, and a mix of botanicals for around 40 days. Then, producers sweeten the liqueur with sugar or syrup before letting it age. Rucolino’s flavor retains the fresh, peppery bite of arugula with bittersweet, herbaceous undertones. Much like other amari, the liqueur is traditionally consumed as a post-meal digestivo.

Sardinia: Mirto

Mirto is a liqueur made with the berries of a myrtle plant, an evergreen shrub indigenous to the Mediterranean. Some accounts suggest Mirto’s production began in Corsica and was later transported to Sardinia, now the home base of the spirit. Many of the island’s inhabitants make batches of Mirto at home for recreational consumption, and only a few professional producers exist. Making the beverage begins with steeping the berries in a high-proof neutral alcohol for up to 60 days. They then strain the liquid, separately press the fruit, and mix in the juice, the volume depending on how much they want to proof the batch down. The ensemble then goes through a final filtration process, resulting in a dark, black currant-colored spirit. The myrtle berries impart their herbal, spicy, and almost savory taste, leading into a lingering, slightly burning finish. The traditional, berry-based Mirto is known as Mirto Rosso. The island also offers Mirto Bianco, made from the less common white variety of the myrtle berries, or the leaves of the plant.

Sicily: Amaro Averna

While Sicily’s beverage scene may be better known for the wines coming from the hot, volcanic slopes of Mount Etna, the island also offers delicious local amari. The history behind Amaro Averna isn’t entirely clear, but the brand suggests monks based in Caltanissetta passed off the original recipe to Salvatore Averna, a textile merchant, in 1868. Later generations of the family continued to build the brand, expanding its popularity worldwide, and eventually turning Fratelli Averna into a corporation in 1958. The Campari Group eventually picked it up in 2014 for €103 million ($120 million) before selling it off, along with Mirto brand Zedda Piras, for €100 million ($116 million). Despite all of the switches in ownership, Amaro Averna’s production still remains faithful to the original 19th-century recipe. The blend of botanicals is a secret, but the liqueur, bottled at 29 percent ABV, brings flavors of citrus, caramel, cola, and herbs. Sicily is also home to a few other artisanal amaro brands that work with local botanicals, including Amaro dell’Etna.
